title: Patterning the Embryonic Nervous System
summary: How signaling molecules turn a flat sheet of embryonic cells into a regionally patterned neural tube.

lessons.title: Neural Induction and BMP Inhibition

levels.kid:
Very early on, a baby animal is just a flat sheet of tiny cells. Some of those cells will become skin. Others will become the brain and spinal cord. How do they know which job to pick?

The cells send each other little chemical messages. One message, called **BMP**, tells cells: "Become skin!" But a special group of helper cells, called the **organizer**, sends out "blockers" that catch the BMP message before it arrives.

Cells that don't hear "become skin" turn into brain cells instead. It's a bit like covering someone's ears so they miss an instruction. Scientists found that becoming a brain cell is what these cells do on their own when nobody tells them otherwise!
levels.hs:
**Neural induction** is the step in early development when part of the embryo's outer layer, the **ectoderm**, is told to become **neural tissue**: the future brain and spinal cord. The rest of the ectoderm becomes **epidermis** (skin).

The key discovery came in 1924. **Hans Spemann and Hilde Mangold** transplanted a small piece of tissue from one newt embryo, the upper lip of the blastopore, into another embryo. The host grew a second body axis, including a second nervous system, mostly built from its own cells. That transplanted tissue became known as the **Spemann organizer**. It doesn't build the new nervous system itself; it *instructs* neighboring cells.

For decades, people searched for the organizer's "make neural" signal. The answer, found in the 1990s, was surprising:
- Ectoderm cells are bathed in **BMP** (bone morphogenetic protein), a signal that pushes them toward skin.
- The organizer secretes **BMP antagonists**: **Noggin**, **Chordin** and **Follistatin**. These proteins bind BMP and stop it from reaching its receptors.
- Ectoderm that is shielded from BMP becomes neural.

This idea is called the **default model**: neural fate is what ectoderm adopts when BMP signaling is blocked. Later work showed other signals help too, but blocking BMP remains central to how the nervous system begins.
levels.college:
Neural induction converts naive ectoderm into **neuroectoderm** (the neural plate) during gastrulation. It is the first decision in nervous system development, preceding neural tube closure and regional patterning.

**The organizer.** Spemann and Mangold's 1924 grafts of the amphibian dorsal blastopore lip induced a secondary axis whose neural tissue came largely from host cells. Equivalent organizers exist across vertebrates: **Hensen's node** in chick and the **node** in mouse.

**Molecular basis: BMP inhibition.**
- **BMP4** (with BMP2/7) is expressed throughout the early ectoderm. It binds type I/II serine-threonine kinase receptors, which phosphorylate **SMAD1/5/8**. These pair with **SMAD4**, enter the nucleus and activate epidermal genes (e.g., *Msx1*, keratins).
- The organizer secretes antagonists that bind BMP ligands directly and block receptor engagement: **Noggin** (Smith & Harland, 1992), **Chordin** (Sasai, De Robertis et al., 1994) and **Follistatin** (Hemmati-Brivanlou, Melton et al., 1994).
- Dissociated *Xenopus* animal-cap cells, which dilute away secreted BMP, become neural. A dominant-negative BMP receptor does the same. These experiments supported the **default model**.

**Beyond default.**
- **FGF** signaling contributes, especially in chick, partly by having MAPK phosphorylate the SMAD1 linker region, which targets SMAD1 for degradation.
- **Wnt** inhibition also helps: Wnt/GSK3 interplay controls SMAD1 stability, and Wnt activity in chick epiblast favors epidermal fate.
- Early neural markers include **Sox2**, **Sox3**, **Zic** genes and **Geminin**.

**Anterior first.** Induced tissue initially has **anterior (forebrain) character**. Posterior identities are added later by "transforming" signals, the activation–transformation idea of Nieuwkoop. That regional patterning is covered in later lessons.

**Relevance.** Stem-cell protocols for making human neurons copy this logic. **Dual-SMAD inhibition** (Chambers et al., 2009) uses Noggin or a small-molecule BMP-receptor blocker together with SB431542 (which blocks TGF-β/Activin/Nodal) to efficiently convert pluripotent stem cells into neuroectoderm.
levels.phd:
The molecular story of neural induction runs from Spemann–Mangold (1924) through a long period in which candidate inducers were confounded by "autoneuralization" artifacts. It was resolved by *Xenopus* animal-cap assays in the early 1990s.

**Key experiments.** Grunz and Tacke (1989) and Godsave and Slack (1989) showed that dispersing animal-cap cells yields neural tissue without any inducer. Hemmati-Brivanlou and Melton found that a truncated activin receptor neuralized caps, initially interpreted as activin blockade. The receptor actually trapped multiple TGF-β-family ligands, including BMPs. Smith and Harland isolated **Noggin** through expression cloning of dorsalizing activity. Sasai and colleagues identified **Chordin**. Zimmerman et al. (1996) and Piccolo et al. (1996) showed that Noggin and Chordin bind BMP4 directly with high affinity, blocking access to the receptor.

**Extracellular regulation.** Chordin's activity is shaped by **Tolloid/Xolloid** metalloproteases, which cleave Chordin and release BMP, and by **Twisted gastrulation**. These interactions create a shuttling system that moves BMP ventrally and forms a dorsoventral gradient. The **ventral center** (BMP4, Xolloid-related, Sizzled, Crossveinless-2) works with the dorsal organizer to make the pattern self-regulating (De Robertis). The mirror-image pathway, **Sog/Dpp**, in *Drosophila*, where the nerve cord is ventral, reflects deep conservation of the BMP–antagonist axis and supports Geoffroy Saint-Hilaire's dorsoventral inversion hypothesis.

**Integration at SMAD1.** De Robertis and colleagues showed that SMAD1 carries out three inputs. BMP receptors phosphorylate its C-terminus (activation). FGF/MAPK phosphorylate its linker region, and GSK3 then adds further linker phosphates, primed by MAPK. Linker phosphorylation recruits Smurf1 for degradation. Wnt, by inhibiting GSK3, stabilizes SMAD1 and so promotes epidermis, so FGF and Wnt inhibition both converge on lowering BMP output.

**Controversy.** In chick, Stern's group showed that BMP antagonists alone fail to neuralize competent epiblast outside the area that will form the neural plate. Neural induction began before node formation and required early FGF (e.g., via *Churchill* and *Sip1/Zeb2*, which represses mesoderm genes). Single Chordin and Noggin mouse knockouts develop a largely normal forebrain, revealing redundancy. The double mutant lacks forebrain (Bachiller et al., 2000), pointing to roles in anterior maintenance more than induction itself. Current consensus: BMP inhibition is necessary but not sufficient in amniotes. It acts in combination with timing, competence and FGF/Wnt cues.
levels.expert:
Neural induction has moved from embryology to working tool, and the most consequential application is directed differentiation.

**Dual-SMAD inhibition in practice.** The Chambers protocol (Noggin or the BMP type I receptor inhibitors dorsomorphin/LDN-193189, plus SB431542 against ALK4/5/7) produces PAX6+ neuroepithelium from human pluripotent stem cells within roughly 10–12 days. Studer's group then layered in patterning factors to derive midbrain dopamine neurons; this lineage now underlies clinical trials of stem-cell-derived cell replacement for Parkinson's disease, including bemdaneprocel (BlueRock/Bayer) and Kyoto iPSC trials, with early safety reports published in 2025. A recurring pitfall is incomplete patterning or contaminating proliferative cells, which carry risks of tumor-like overgrowth and off-target neurons. As a result, release criteria now include extensive marker profiling and single-cell transcriptomics.

**Organoids.** Cerebral organoids (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2013) depend on the same anterior-default logic: minimally patterned neuroectoderm drifts toward forebrain identity. Protocols that add dual-SMAD inhibition produce more reproducible cortical organoids, while unguided methods show batch-to-batch variability in regional identity. This is important when modeling patient-specific microcephaly or autism variants, where an apparent phenotype may actually reflect a patterning artifact. Isogenic controls and multiple lines are essential.

**Human genetics.** Complete loss of core inducers is presumably incompatible with development, but partial pathway lesions reach the clinic. **NOG** variants cause proximal symphalangism and multiple synostosis syndromes, showing that skeletal BMP regulation is dosage-sensitive. Heterozygous **ZEB2** loss causes **Mowat–Wilson syndrome** (intellectual disability, Hirschsprung disease, characteristic facial features). ZEB2 is a SMAD-interacting repressor active in early neural tissue. *ZIC2* variants are associated with holoprosencephaly, a midline and patterning disorder. Gain-of-function *ACVR1* (FOP) illustrates how BMP receptor activity extends well beyond early embryo patterning.

**Open questions.**
- How is ectodermal competence encoded? Pluripotency factors (OCT4/POU5F1, SOX2) and early chromatin states may prime neural fate before signals arrive.
- How do embryos make neural-versus-epidermal decisions sharp despite noisy morphogen levels?
- Do human gastruloids and embryo models validate amniote-specific mechanisms, given that ethics constraints limit direct study of human embryos?

For surgeons, the practical lesson is that very early signaling errors set the stage for structural brain anomalies encountered decades later.

keyPoints: Neural induction turns part of the ectoderm into the neural plate
Spemann and Mangold's 1924 organizer graft induced a second nervous system
BMP4 signaling through SMAD1/5/8 pushes ectoderm toward epidermis
The organizer secretes Noggin, Chordin and Follistatin, which bind and block BMP
Default model: ectoderm becomes neural when BMP is blocked; FGF and Wnt inhibition help
Dual-SMAD inhibition copies this logic to make neurons from stem cells

test.q: Which germ layer gives rise to the neural plate during neural induction?
test.explain: Neural tissue and epidermis both come from the ectoderm; neural induction decides between them.

A secondary body axis with a nervous system
A tumor made of grafted cells

test.explain: BMP pushes ectoderm toward skin; blocking it allows neural fate.

test.q: How do Noggin and Chordin work?

They activate BMP type I receptors
They bind BMP ligands outside cells
They degrade BMP mRNA inside cells

test.explain: BMP receptors phosphorylate SMAD1/5/8, which partner with SMAD4. SMAD2/3 belong to the TGF-β/Activin branch.

The cells start to make retinoic acid

test.q: What is the chick and mammalian equivalent of the amphibian organizer?
test.explain: Hensen's node (chick) and the node (mouse) are the amniote organizers.

test.q: Newly induced neural tissue initially has what regional character?
test.explain: Induced neuroectoderm starts anterior (forebrain); posterior identities are added by later signals.

test.q: Dual-SMAD inhibition pairs a BMP blocker with SB431542, which blocks:
test.explain: SB431542 inhibits the Activin/Nodal/TGF-β receptors that signal via SMAD2/3, the second SMAD branch.

test.q: Name the BMP antagonist cloned by Smith and Harland in 1992.
test.explain: Noggin was found through expression cloning for dorsalizing activity in Xenopus.

test.q: The idea that ectoderm becomes neural when BMP is blocked is called the ___ model.
test.explain: Neural fate is the default when no BMP signal is received.

test.q: What is the name for the tissue whose graft induces a second axis?
test.explain: The Spemann organizer instructs surrounding tissue.

kidTest.q: What does the BMP message tell early cells?
kidTest.explain: BMP tells cells to become skin.

kidTest.q: What does the organizer send out?
kidTest.explain: The organizer's blockers catch BMP before it arrives.

kidTest.q: Cells that don't hear 'become skin' turn into:
kidTest.explain: Without the skin message, cells become brain and spinal cord cells.

kidTest.q: What does the very early embryo look like?
kidTest.explain: It starts as a flat sheet of cells.

kidTest.q: The helper cells that block BMP are called the o _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The organizer sends blockers to make brain cells.

advancedTest.q: Why does Wnt inhibition favor neural fate at the level of SMAD1?
choices: Wnt signaling prevents Noggin from binding to BMP4 ligand
Active GSK3 adds linker phosphates that degrade SMAD1
Wnt ligands directly phosphorylate the SMAD1 C-terminus
GSK3 inhibition raises transcription of the BMP4 gene
advancedTest.explain: Without Wnt, GSK3 phosphorylates the SMAD1 linker (after MAPK priming), recruiting Smurf1 for degradation and lowering BMP output.

advancedTest.q: Chordin;Noggin double mutant mice lack forebrain yet form neural tissue. What does this best suggest?
choices: BMP antagonists are irrelevant to neural development
Follistatin is the main mammalian neural inducer
Neural induction in mice depends on Sonic hedgehog
They act redundantly, especially in anterior maintenance
advancedTest.explain: Single mutants are mild; the double mutant's forebrain loss shows redundancy and a key role in maintaining anterior tissue, not sole responsibility for induction.

advancedTest.q: Stern's chick experiments challenged the default model because:
choices: BMP signaling was found to promote neural fate in chick
Chick neural tissue was found to arise from the endoderm
BMP antagonists alone did not neuralize the epiblast
The chick genome lacks any recognizable homolog of Chordin
advancedTest.explain: Antagonists were insufficient outside the prospective neural area; earlier FGF signals and competence were also required.

advancedTest.q: An unguided cortical organoid line shows a 'phenotype' that disappears with dual-SMAD inhibition. The likeliest explanation is:
choices: Variable regional patterning was the source
The patient variant was a de novo mutation
BMP inhibition causes microcephaly in organoids
SB431542 corrects the patient's genetic variant
advancedTest.explain: Unguided organoids vary in regional identity; a difference resolved by stronger induction suggests a patterning artifact, hence the need for isogenic controls.

lessons.title: Neural Tube Closure, Folate and Neural Tube Defects

levels.kid:
Early in a baby's life, long before it looks like a baby, the part that will become the brain and spinal cord starts as a flat sheet of cells. Then the edges of the sheet lift up and fold together, like rolling a flat taco shell into a tube. This is called the **neural tube**.

The tube must zip closed all the way. The top end becomes the brain. The long part becomes the spinal cord.

Sometimes the zipper does not close all the way. That leaves an opening, which can hurt the spinal cord or brain. Doctors call this a **neural tube defect**.

A vitamin called **folate** (found in leafy greens) helps the zipper close. That is why moms are told to get enough folate even before a baby starts growing.
levels.hs:
The brain and spinal cord begin as the **neural plate**, a flat sheet of cells on the back of the embryo. During **neurulation**, the plate's edges (the **neural folds**) rise, bend toward each other and fuse in the midline, forming the hollow **neural tube**. This happens remarkably early, in the third and fourth weeks after conception, often before a person knows they are pregnant.

Closure starts in the region of the future neck and zips toward both ends. The head-end opening (the **anterior neuropore**) closes around day 25, and the tail-end opening (the **posterior neuropore**) around day 27-28.

If closure fails, the result is a **neural tube defect (NTD)**:
- **Anencephaly**: the head end fails to close, so most of the brain and skull do not develop. It is fatal.
- **Spina bifida**: the lower end fails to close. In its severe form, **myelomeningocele**, the spinal cord and its coverings protrude through the back, causing leg weakness and bladder problems.

**Folate** (vitamin B9; its synthetic form is **folic acid**) is needed to make DNA for the rapidly dividing cells. Real example: after the United States required folic acid fortification of enriched grain in 1998, NTD rates fell by roughly a quarter to a third. Because closure happens so early, folic acid works best when taken before conception.
levels.college:
**Mechanics of neurulation.** Primary neurulation converts the neural plate into a tube through coordinated cell behaviors:
- **Convergent extension**: cells intercalate mediolaterally, narrowing and lengthening the plate. This is driven by the **planar cell polarity (PCP)** pathway (genes such as *VANGL1/2*, *CELSR1*, *SCRIB*).
- **Hinge points**: a **medial hinge point** over the notochord and paired **dorsolateral hinge points** bend the plate. Apical constriction, powered by actomyosin and the protein **Shroom3**, wedges the cells.
- **Fold elevation and fusion**: the folds meet, and surface ectoderm cells form protrusions that zip them together. The neural tube then separates from the overlying ectoderm, and **neural crest** cells delaminate from the fold edges.

The lowest sacral and coccygeal cord forms differently, by **secondary neurulation**: a mesenchymal cord cavitates. Defects there are usually *closed* (skin-covered) dysraphisms.

**Classifying NTDs.**
- **Open**: anencephaly, myelomeningocele, craniorachischisis (the whole tube fails to close).
- **Closed/skin-covered**: lipomyelomeningocele, spina bifida occulta, tethered cord.
- **Encephalocele**: a post-closure herniation of brain through a skull defect.

**Folate biology.** Folate carries one-carbon units for thymidylate and purine synthesis and, through methionine, for **S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)**, the universal methyl donor. The common **MTHFR C677T** variant mildly reduces enzyme activity and modestly raises NTD risk. The MRC Vitamin Study (1991) showed folic acid prevented about 72% of recurrences in women with a previously affected pregnancy.

**Screening.** Open NTDs leak **alpha-fetoprotein (AFP)**, which is raised in maternal serum and amniotic fluid. Ultrasound shows the "lemon" (scalloped frontal bones) and "banana" (cerebellum) signs.

**Teratogens.** **Valproate** and **carbamazepine**, maternal diabetes, obesity and hyperthermia all raise NTD risk.
levels.phd:
**Closure points and cellular machinery.** In mice, closure initiates at discrete sites: **Closure 1** at the hindbrain/cervical boundary, **Closure 2** at the forebrain/midbrain boundary, and **Closure 3** at the rostral forebrain. Zippering proceeds between them. Failure of Closure 1 gives craniorachischisis, and incomplete zippering yields anencephaly or spina bifida. Human closure sites are debated, and evidence suggests fewer discrete sites than in mice. Mouse strain differences in Closure 2 position change exencephaly susceptibility, an early clue that NTDs are polygenic.

**PCP and craniorachischisis.** The *loop-tail* (*Vangl2*) and *crash* (*Celsr1*) mutants have open neural tubes from midbrain to tail because convergent extension fails. The plate stays too wide for the folds to meet. Rare heterozygous missense variants in *VANGL1/2*, *CELSR1*, *SCRIB* and *FZD6* are found in human NTD cohorts, but penetrance is low.

**Dorsolateral hinge point regulation.** Sonic hedgehog from the notochord inhibits dorsolateral bending, while BMP antagonists such as Noggin promote it. This explains why *Shh*-pathway overactivation (for example, *Ptch1* loss) causes NTDs. Ventral patterning by Shh is a separate topic covered later.

**Folate: an incompletely solved mechanism.** Folic acid prevents a large fraction of human NTDs, but the mechanism remains unresolved. Candidate explanations are impaired nucleotide supply, which slows proliferation in the rapidly expanding neuroepithelium, and reduced methylation capacity. Key evidence:
- Mitochondrial one-carbon metabolism matters. **Glycine cleavage system** genes (*AMT*, *GLDC*) are mutated in some human NTDs, and *Gldc*-null mice get NTDs that are rescued by formate.
- Some mouse NTDs are folate-*resistant* but respond to **inositol** (for example, *curly tail*, a *Grhl3* hypomorph).
- Folate receptor 1 (*Folr1*) knockout mice show NTDs.

**Epidemiology.** Fortification programs (US/Canada 1998, Chile 2000) reduced NTD prevalence by roughly 20-50%, with larger drops where baseline rates were high. A residual floor of about 5-6 per 10,000 births may be folate-resistant. Recurrence risk after one affected child is about 2-5%, consistent with multifactorial inheritance.
levels.expert:
**Fetal surgery.** The MOMS trial (Adzick et al., NEJM 2011) randomized prenatal (before 26 weeks) versus postnatal repair of myelomeningocele. Prenatal repair roughly halved the need for CSF shunting (about 40% versus 82% receiving a shunt). It also improved hindbrain herniation and motor function, and doubled the rate of independent walking at 30 months. The trade-offs are higher rates of preterm birth and uterine-scar dehiscence. This supports the **"two-hit" hypothesis**: the primary closure defect is followed by secondary damage to the exposed cord from amniotic fluid and trauma, which is what makes in-utero coverage worthwhile. Fetoscopic approaches now aim to reduce maternal morbidity, and outcome equivalence is still being established. Stem-cell-augmented patches are in early trials.

**Neurosurgical sequelae.** Nearly all children with myelomeningocele have a **Chiari II malformation**. CSF leakage through the open defect is thought to collapse the developing ventricular system and posterior fossa. Lifelong issues include hydrocephalus and shunt failure, **secondary tethered cord** (new scoliosis, worsening gait or bladder function), syringomyelia and latex allergy. Shunt malfunction can present subtly, such as declining school performance or new swallowing difficulty from brainstem compression.

**Occult dysraphism.** Midline lumbosacral skin markers raise suspicion: a hair tuft, subcutaneous lipoma, hemangioma, a dimple above the gluteal crease, or a deviated gluteal cleft. These warrant spinal ultrasound in early infancy (while the posterior elements are unossified) or MRI later. A simple low dimple within the cleft usually needs no imaging.

**Pharmacology pitfalls.** Valproate carries roughly a 10-20-fold rise in spina bifida risk and also affects neurodevelopment. Regulators (EMA, MHRA) now restrict its use in people who could become pregnant. Valproate inhibits histone deacetylases, and whether it acts mainly through folate is unclear. Folate antagonists (methotrexate, trimethoprim) are also implicated. Prevention guidance uses higher folic acid for high-risk pregnancies.

**Open questions.** The remaining questions include the identity of folate-resistant NTDs, the role of B12 status and of the FOLR1 autoantibodies reported in some mothers, and gene-environment interactions in polygenic risk. Global fortification gaps also remain: many countries still lack mandatory programs, leaving an estimated large preventable burden.

keyPoints: Neural folds elevate and fuse to form the neural tube in weeks 3-4
Anterior neuropore closes ~day 25, posterior ~day 27-28
Anencephaly = cranial failure; myelomeningocele = caudal open spina bifida
Planar cell polarity drives convergent extension; mutants get craniorachischisis
Folic acid before conception prevents many NTDs; fortification cut rates
Prenatal repair (MOMS trial) reduced shunting; Chiari II accompanies myelomeningocele

test.q: During which weeks after conception does the neural tube close?
test.explain: Neurulation occurs in weeks 3-4, often before pregnancy is recognized. That is why folic acid should be taken before conception.

test.q: Failure of the head end of the neural tube to close causes:
test.explain: Anterior neuropore failure produces anencephaly. Spina bifida results from failure at the caudal end.

test.q: Myelomeningocele is best described as:
choices: A skull defect with herniated brain
Open spina bifida with exposed cord
Failure of the whole tube to close
test.explain: Myelomeningocele is the severe open form of spina bifida. The other options describe encephalocele, lipomyelomeningocele and craniorachischisis.

test.q: Which pathway drives convergent extension of the neural plate?
test.explain: PCP genes such as VANGL2 and CELSR1 drive mediolateral intercalation. When this fails, the plate stays too wide to close.

test.q: Folate supports neural tube closure mainly by supplying:
test.explain: Folate carries one-carbon units for nucleotide synthesis and methylation, which rapidly dividing neuroepithelium needs.

test.q: Which maternal serum marker is raised in open neural tube defects?
test.explain: AFP leaks from the exposed neural tissue, raising its level in maternal serum and amniotic fluid.

test.q: Which antiseizure drug is a well-known NTD teratogen?
test.explain: Valproate markedly increases spina bifida risk. Carbamazepine is also implicated.

test.q: The lowest sacral cord forms by secondary neurulation, so defects there are usually:
test.explain: Secondary neurulation, in which a mesenchymal cord cavitates, tends to give closed dysraphisms such as tethered cord.

test.q: Which brain malformation accompanies nearly all myelomeningoceles?
test.explain: CSF leakage through the open defect is thought to cause hindbrain herniation, known as Chiari II.

test.q: The flat sheet that rolls up into the neural tube is the neural ___.
test.explain: The neural plate's folds elevate and fuse to make the tube.

test.q: What is the synthetic form of vitamin B9 used in supplements and fortification?
test.explain: Folic acid is the synthetic form; folate is the natural form found in foods.

test.q: The tail-end opening of the neural tube is the posterior ___.
test.explain: The posterior neuropore closes around day 27-28. When it fails to close, spina bifida results.

kidTest.q: What does the flat sheet of cells fold into?
kidTest.explain: It rolls up into the neural tube.

kidTest.q: What does the top end of the tube become?
kidTest.explain: The top end becomes the brain, and the long part becomes the spinal cord.

kidTest.q: What is it called when the tube does not close all the way?
kidTest.explain: An opening left in the tube is a neural tube defect.

kidTest.q: Where can you find folate?
kidTest.explain: Leafy green vegetables contain folate.

kidTest.q: Which vitamin helps the tube close? f _ _ _ _ _
kidTest.explain: Folate helps the neural tube zip shut.

advancedTest.q: Vangl2 loop-tail mice have an open tube from midbrain to tail. The best explanation is:
choices: A plate too wide for the folds to meet
Excess Shh blocking dorsolateral hinge points
advancedTest.explain: PCP loss prevents convergent extension, so the plate stays wide and Closure 1 fails, giving craniorachischisis.

advancedTest.q: The curly tail mouse responds to inositol but not folic acid. This implies that:
choices: Folate deficiency causes most mouse NTDs
Inositol works by raising folate levels in tissue
Some NTDs arise through folate-independent routes
Curly tail mice lack the glycine cleavage enzyme
advancedTest.explain: Folate-resistant, inositol-responsive NTDs show that multiple pathways cause NTDs. This fits a residual folate-resistant floor in humans.

advancedTest.q: Which finding most directly supports the two-hit hypothesis underlying prenatal repair?
choices: Recurrence risk is about 2-5% after one child
AFP is raised in amniotic fluid in open defects
Fetal coverage reduces shunting and hindbrain herniation
MTHFR C677T modestly raises population NTD risk
advancedTest.explain: If damage were entirely primary, covering the cord in utero would not improve outcomes. The MOMS trial benefits imply that secondary injury is preventable.

advancedTest.q: Gldc-null mice develop NTDs that formate rescues. This points to a key role for:
choices: Planar cell polarity signaling in the plate
advancedTest.explain: Formate supplies one-carbon units downstream of the glycine cleavage system. Rescue by formate implicates mitochondrial one-carbon supply.

lessons.title: Sonic Hedgehog and Dorsoventral Patterning

levels.kid:
Imagine a long tube made of tiny cells. It will grow up to become your spinal cord. But how does each cell know what job to take?

At the bottom of the tube, special cells send out a chemical message called **Sonic hedgehog**. Yes, scientists named it after the video game character!

The message is like the smell of cookies baking. Near the oven, the smell is strong. Far away, it is faint. Cells close to the bottom get a strong message, and many of them become cells that help you **move** your muscles. Cells farther up get a weak message and become different cells.

The top of the tube sends its own message too. Cells near the top become cells that help you **feel** things like touch.
levels.hs:
After the neural tube forms, its cells must become different kinds of neurons depending on their position. The bottom (ventral) side will make **motor neurons**, which control muscles. The top (dorsal) side will make neurons that handle **sensory** information.

The key ventral signal is a protein called **Sonic hedgehog (Shh)**. It is first released by the **notochord**, a rod of tissue lying just beneath the neural tube. Shh tells the nearby bottom cells of the tube to become the **floor plate**, which then makes Shh too.

Shh spreads upward and forms a **gradient**: high near the floor plate, lower farther away. A signaling molecule that gives different instructions at different concentrations is called a **morphogen**.

- Highest Shh: floor plate cells
- High Shh: certain ventral interneurons
- Moderate Shh: motor neurons
- Low or no Shh: more dorsal cell types

Meanwhile the **roof plate** at the top releases opposing signals, **BMPs** and **Wnts**, which push cells toward dorsal fates.

Why it matters: when Shh signaling fails early in development, the forebrain may not split into left and right halves. This condition, **holoprosencephaly**, can come with facial differences such as closely set eyes. In its most severe form, there is a single central eye. This was first linked to Shh when lambs born to sheep that ate a wild plant called corn lily developed it.
levels.college:
Dorsoventral (DV) patterning of the spinal cord is the classic model of morphogen-based patterning in vertebrates.

**Sources.** The notochord secretes Shh and induces the overlying ventral midline to become the **floor plate**, a second Shh source. Dorsally, the roof plate and overlying ectoderm provide **BMPs** and **Wnts**.

**The protein.** Shh is synthesized as a precursor that cleaves itself. The active N-terminal fragment carries a **cholesterol** group, and a **palmitate** is added by the enzyme Hhat. These lipids tether Shh to membranes. Release needs the transporter **Dispatched** plus the secreted helper **Scube2**.

**Pathway.**
- With no Shh, the receptor **Patched1 (Ptch1)** keeps **Smoothened (Smo)** inactive.
- Shh binds Ptch1, relieving this inhibition. Smo then accumulates in the **primary cilium**.
- Downstream, **Gli** transcription factors change state. Gli2 is the main activator. Gli3 is mostly processed into a repressor when Shh is absent. **SuFu** restrains Gli proteins.
- Ptch1 and Hhip are Shh target genes, so signaling creates negative feedback.

**Reading the gradient.** Shh controls two classes of homeodomain transcription factors:
- **Class I** genes are repressed by Shh (Pax7, Pax6, Dbx1/2, Irx3).
- **Class II** genes are induced by Shh (Nkx6.1, Olig2, Nkx2.2).

Pairs of these factors repress each other: Pax6 with Nkx2.2, and Irx3 with Olig2. This **cross-repression** turns a smooth gradient into sharp progenitor domains: p0, p1, p2, pMN and p3 from dorsal to ventral. The **pMN** domain (Olig2+, Nkx6.1+, lacking Irx3 and Nkx2.2) makes motor neurons and later oligodendrocytes. The p3 domain (Nkx2.2+) makes V3 interneurons.

**Human relevance.** **SHH** mutations are the most common single-gene cause of holoprosencephaly. Inherited **PTCH1** loss causes Gorlin syndrome, with medulloblastoma and basal cell carcinoma risk.
levels.phd:
Classic work from the Jessell and Briscoe labs established ventral neural tube patterning as a paradigm for morphogen interpretation. Ericson and colleagues showed in neural plate explants that graded Shh concentrations, spanning only a few fold, induce distinct ventral identities. Briscoe et al. (Cell, 2000) defined the class I/II code and showed that misexpressing one partner of a cross-repressive pair displaces the domain boundary. This means the transcription factors themselves sharpen and position boundaries.

**Gli code.** Ventral identity depends on the balance of Gli activator and repressor (GliA/GliR), not simply on ligand concentration. In Shh-/- embryos the ventral neural tube is lost. In Shh-/-;Gli3-/- double mutants, many ventral progenitor domains, including pMN and p2, are substantially restored, although their boundaries are disorganized. So a major job of Shh is to prevent Gli3R formation. The floor plate and p3 still need Gli2 activator.

**Temporal adaptation.** Dessaud et al. (Nature, 2007) showed that cells integrate both concentration and **duration** of exposure. Ptch1 upregulation desensitizes cells over time, so a given ligand level gives progressively lower Gli activity. Brief exposure to a high concentration yields more dorsal fates than sustained exposure. Ventral fates therefore need sustained signaling.

**Network dynamics.** Balaskas et al. (Cell, 2012) modeled the Pax6–Olig2–Nkx2.2 circuit as a gene regulatory network with **hysteresis**. Once Nkx2.2 is established, it can persist even if Shh falls. The network converts a transient, noisy gradient into stable, bistable domains. Opposing BMP/Wnt input from the roof plate and Shh-independent retinoic acid input from paraxial mesoderm help position domains and scale them as the tube grows.

**Cilia.** Mouse forward genetic screens (Huangfu, Anderson et al., 2003) found intraflagellar transport (IFT) mutants with ventral patterning defects. In vertebrates Smo trafficking, Gli activation and Gli3 processing all occur in the primary cilium. Loss of IFT removes both GliA and GliR, so mutants lose the most ventral fates while intermediate fates can persist.

**Reception.** Co-receptors **Cdon, Boc and Gas1** enhance Shh binding. Triple mutants resemble Shh nulls. Hhip and Ptch1 also sequester ligand, sculpting the gradient's range.
levels.expert:
**Holoprosencephaly (HPE)** is the most direct human readout of failed ventral midline patterning. Its prevalence is roughly 1 in 10,000 births but far higher in early pregnancy loss. Beyond SHH, implicated genes include ZIC2, SIX3, TGIF1, GLI2, CDON and DISP1. Penetrance is strikingly variable: relatives carrying the same SHH variant may show anything from alobar HPE to a lone single central incisor or no findings. This supports a **multiple-hit model**, where gene dosage combines with modifier variants and environmental factors. The genetics recall the **cyclopamine** story: this Veratrum californicum alkaloid binds Smo directly. Defects of cholesterol synthesis, notably **Smith–Lemli–Opitz syndrome** (DHCR7), can include HPE, plausibly through impaired Smo activation by sterols.

**Ciliopathies.** Joubert syndrome and Meckel–Gruber syndrome link ciliary protein variants to midline and hindbrain malformations, partly via disturbed Hedgehog transduction.

**Oncology.** Shh is also a mitogen for cerebellar granule neuron precursors. Constitutive pathway activation drives the **SHH-activated medulloblastoma** subgroup. Here the lesion's position in the pathway predicts drug response:
- PTCH1 or SMO mutations: potentially sensitive to SMO inhibitors (vismodegib, sonidegib).
- SUFU loss or GLI2/MYCN amplification: downstream of SMO, so intrinsically resistant.

SMO inhibitors are approved for advanced basal cell carcinoma. Pediatric use is limited because young animals and children have shown irreversible **premature growth-plate fusion**. Acquired SMO resistance mutations further limit durability, driving interest in GLI-directed approaches.

**Beyond fate specification.** Floor-plate Shh also attracts commissural axons toward the midline, acting through Smo (with Boc as receptor) rather than the canonical transcriptional route (Charron et al., 2003; Okada et al., 2006). This illustrates noncanonical signaling.

**Research tools.** Embryonic stem cell differentiation protocols set retinoic acid and SMO agonist exposure to generate human motor neurons. These are widely used to model ALS and spinal muscular atrophy, a direct translation of DV-patterning logic.

Open questions include how gradients scale with tissue growth, how cell-to-cell variability is buffered, and whether human-specific features alter interpretation timing.

keyPoints: Notochord and floor plate secrete Sonic hedgehog, a ventral morphogen
Roof plate BMPs and Wnts oppose Shh and promote dorsal fates
Shh binds Patched, freeing Smoothened to signal via Gli in the primary cilium
Class I genes are repressed and class II genes induced by Shh
Cross-repression between transcription factors sharpens progenitor domains like pMN
Failed Shh signaling causes holoprosencephaly; overactivity drives some tumors

test.q: Which tissue is the first source of Shh for the ventral neural tube?
test.explain: The notochord beneath the neural tube secretes Shh and induces the floor plate. The roof plate provides dorsal signals instead.

test.q: Which protein does Shh bind directly to start signaling?
test.explain: Shh binds Patched1, which relieves Patched's inhibition of Smoothened. Smoothened is the signal transducer, not the ligand-binding receptor.

test.q: Cells exposed to the highest levels of Shh become:
test.explain: The floor plate forms at the highest Shh levels. Motor neurons form at moderate levels, slightly farther from the midline.

test.q: Which signals from the roof plate oppose Shh and promote dorsal identity?
test.explain: The roof plate secretes BMPs and Wnts, which push cells toward dorsal fates.

test.q: A transcription factor gene that is repressed by Shh, such as Pax6, belongs to which group?
test.explain: Class I genes (Pax6, Pax7, Irx3, Dbx) are repressed by Shh; class II genes like Nkx2.2 and Olig2 are induced.

test.q: Inside the responding cell, the Shh pathway ultimately acts through which transcription factors?
test.explain: Gli2 acts mainly as an activator, and Gli3 mainly as a repressor when Shh is absent. Smads carry BMP signals.

test.q: Loss of SHH function in a human embryo is a classic cause of:
test.explain: SHH mutations are the most common single-gene cause of holoprosencephaly, in which the forebrain fails to divide into two halves.

test.q: Vertebrate Shh signal transduction depends on which cell structure?
test.explain: Smoothened moves into the primary cilium, where Gli activation and Gli3 processing take place.

test.q: Sharp boundaries between ventral progenitor domains arise mainly because:
choices: Shh spreads evenly across the whole neural tube
Roof plate cells die off at each boundary
Paired transcription factors repress each other
Cells sort by migrating away from the notochord region
test.explain: Cross-repression between pairs like Pax6/Nkx2.2 and Irx3/Olig2 converts a smooth gradient into sharp domains.

test.q: Which lipid, attached to the Shh protein, helps tether it to membranes?
test.explain: The active Shh fragment carries cholesterol (and a palmitate), which limits and controls its spread.

test.q: The plant alkaloid cyclopamine blocks Shh signaling by binding ___.
test.explain: Cyclopamine binds Smoothened directly, explaining the cyclopic lambs born to sheep that ate corn lily.

test.q: The Olig2-expressing pMN domain produces ___ neurons and later oligodendrocytes.
test.explain: pMN progenitors (Olig2+, Nkx6.1+) generate motor neurons, then switch to making oligodendrocytes.

kidTest.q: Where does the Sonic hedgehog message come from?
kidTest.explain: Special cells at the bottom of the tube send out the message.

kidTest.q: Many cells near the bottom, with a strong message, become cells that help you:
kidTest.explain: A strong message near the bottom makes many cells into movement cells.

kidTest.q: Where did the name Sonic hedgehog come from?
kidTest.explain: Scientists named it after the video game character Sonic.

kidTest.q: How does a cell know which job to take?
choices: By the color of the cell
By how old the cell has grown
By how strong the message is
kidTest.explain: Like a cookie smell, the message is strong close by and faint far away, and cells read that.

kidTest.q: The cells are in a long t _ _ _ that becomes the spinal cord.
kidTest.explain: The neural tube grows up to become the spinal cord and brain.

advancedTest.q: Shh-/-;Gli3-/- double mutants regain many ventral progenitor domains that Shh-/- mutants lack. The best interpretation is:
choices: Gli3 secretes a second ligand that replaces Shh in the tube
Gli3 is the main activator needed to form the floor plate
Ventral identity depends on Gli3 activator at peak Shh levels
A major role of Shh is preventing formation of Gli3 repressor
advancedTest.explain: Removing Gli3 removes the repressor that Shh normally prevents, so intermediate ventral fates return. The floor plate still requires Gli2 activator, so Gli3 is not its key activator.

advancedTest.q: Explants given a brief pulse of high Shh adopt more dorsal fates than explants kept in that dose for longer. This supports:
choices: Cross-repression being independent of Shh history
Shh acting as a simple on–off switch for ventral fate
BMP from the explant overriding Shh at high levels
Cells integrating both concentration and exposure duration
advancedTest.explain: Dessaud et al. showed temporal adaptation: sustained signaling is needed for ventral fates, because Ptch1 upregulation desensitizes cells over time.

advancedTest.q: A mouse lacking an intraflagellar transport protein loses both Gli activator and Gli repressor. The predicted neural tube phenotype is:
choices: Normal patterning, since cilia mainly affect sensory cells
Loss of the most ventral fates with some intermediate fates kept
Full dorsalization with the ventral domains lost
Ventral expansion of the floor plate across the tube
advancedTest.explain: Without cilia, peak GliA is lost (no floor plate or p3), but the absence of Gli3R lets intermediate ventral fates persist.

advancedTest.q: Which SHH-subgroup medulloblastoma is least likely to respond to a Smoothened inhibitor?
choices: A tumor with SUFU loss or GLI2 amplification
A tumor with a PTCH1 loss-of-function mutation
A tumor arising in a patient with Gorlin syndrome
A tumor with an activating SMO mutation
advancedTest.explain: SUFU loss and GLI2 amplification act downstream of SMO, so blocking SMO cannot shut the pathway off. PTCH1 and SMO lesions are upstream or at the drug target.

lessons.title: Hox Genes and Hindbrain Segmentation

levels.kid:
Imagine building a long train out of boxes. Each box needs a label so you know what goes inside: one for food, one for toys, one for books.

The back part of a growing baby's brain, called the **hindbrain**, starts out as a tube. Then it splits into a row of little boxes called **rhombomeres**. There are about eight of them.

Special genes called **Hox genes** work like labels. Each box gets its own mix of labels. The labels tell the cells, "You will become the nerve for chewing," or "You will help with breathing."

If a label is missing, a box can get mixed up and build the wrong thing. That is why these tiny labels matter so much.
levels.hs:
The **hindbrain** (rhombencephalon) is the back part of the embryonic brain. It becomes the pons, medulla and cerebellum, which control breathing, heart rate, swallowing and facial movement.

Early in development the hindbrain divides into about eight segments called **rhombomeres** (r1 to r8). Each one is a small compartment, and cells in one rhombomere do not mix with cells in the next. This segmentation is temporary. It lays out a plan for where nerves will form.

What gives each segment its identity? **Hox genes**. These genes code for **transcription factors**, proteins that switch other genes on or off. Humans have 39 Hox genes arranged in four clusters (HOXA, HOXB, HOXC, HOXD).

They have a remarkable property called **colinearity**. Genes at one end of a cluster are switched on toward the head. Genes further along are switched on further back. So the order of the genes on the chromosome matches their order along the body.

One key signal controlling Hox genes is **retinoic acid**, a molecule made from vitamin A. Too much or too little retinoic acid shifts Hox patterns. This is why excess vitamin A derivatives, like the acne drug isotretinoin, can cause birth defects of the hindbrain, face and heart.

Real example: each cranial nerve comes from specific rhombomeres. The facial nerve (VII) motor neurons are born in r4.
levels.college:
**Segmentation.** Around embryonic week 4 in humans (E8.5–E9.5 in mouse), the hindbrain forms transient bulges, rhombomeres r1–r8. They are true **compartments**: boundary cells restrict intermixing, and lineage tracing shows clones respect boundaries. Segmentation creates a two-segment periodicity. Branchiomotor nuclei arise in pairs: the trigeminal (V) from r2–r3, the facial (VII) from r4–r5, the glossopharyngeal (IX) from r6–r7.

**Hox code.** Hox genes encode homeodomain transcription factors. Mammals have 39 genes in four clusters (Hoxa–d) and 13 paralog groups. Three colinearity rules apply:
- **Spatial**: 3' genes (paralog groups 1–4 in the hindbrain) are expressed more anteriorly.
- **Temporal**: 3' genes switch on earlier.
- **Sensitivity**: 3' genes respond to lower retinoic acid levels.

r1 expresses no Hox genes, and Gbx2/Fgf8 at the isthmus pattern it instead. Hoxa2 reaches r2. Hoxb1 marks r4. Groups 3 and 4 reach r5 and r7 boundaries respectively.

**Upstream regulators.**
- **Retinoic acid (RA)**: made by Raldh2 in paraxial mesoderm and degraded anteriorly by Cyp26 enzymes. This produces a posterior-high gradient. RA acts through RAR/RXR receptors that bind retinoic acid response elements (RAREs) near Hox genes.
- **Krox20 (Egr2)**: zinc finger factor expressed in r3 and r5. It is required for those segments and directly activates Hoxa2, Hoxb2 and Hoxb3.
- **MafB (kreisler)**: expressed in r5–r6 and activates Hoxa3/Hoxb3.

**Boundaries.** Eph receptors and ephrins are expressed in alternating rhombomeres (EphA4 in r3/r5, ephrinB ligands in r2/r4/r6). Their bidirectional repulsion sharpens boundaries and prevents cell mixing.

**Neural crest.** Crest from r4 carries Hoxa2/Hoxb2 into pharyngeal arch 2. In Hoxa2-null mice, arch 2 skeleton converts to an arch 1-like duplicate, a **homeotic transformation**.
levels.phd:
**Gene regulatory logic.** Hindbrain segmentation emerges from an interaction between graded RA signaling and cross-regulatory transcription factor networks that convert the gradient into sharp, stable domains. Hoxb1 is the paradigm. A 3' RARE drives early broad expression up to the r3/4 boundary. Hoxb1 then maintains itself in r4 through an autoregulatory element containing Hox–Pbx–Prep (Meis) binding sites. Meanwhile, a 3' repressor element and the RAREs work with Krox20 to silence it in r3/r5. Pbx/Meis TALE homeodomain cofactors increase Hox DNA-binding specificity. Zebrafish *lazarus* (pbx4) mutants lose segmental identity, which shows how essential they are.

**Krox20 bistability.** Krox20 is initiated in r3/r5 by an element responsive to MafB and FGF. It is then locked on by direct positive autoregulation (element A). Bouchoucha et al. modeled this as a bistable switch with community effects that explains the odd/even alternation. Krox20 also represses Hoxb1 and promotes EphA4 expression, linking identity to compartment sorting.

**Chromatin mechanism.** Temporal colinearity correlates with progressive 3'→5' transition of Hox clusters from Polycomb-repressed (H3K27me3) to active chromatin. Duboule and colleagues showed this using 4C/Hi-C as two TAD-like domains flanking each cluster. RA-induced activation of 3' genes involves chromatin decompaction (Chambeyron & Bickmore).

**Classic studies.** Lumsden and Keynes (1989) defined rhombomeres as lineage-restricted units in chick. Wilkinson and Krumlauf mapped Hox expression to rhombomeric boundaries. Rijli et al. (1993) and Gendron-Maguire et al. (1993) showed Hoxa2 loss transforms arch 2 to arch 1. Hoxb1 knockouts fail to specify r4 facial branchiomotor neurons, which then fail their characteristic caudal migration.

**Nuance.** Paralog redundancy complicates genetic analysis. Hoxa1/Hoxb1 double mutants lose r4 identity and r5 more severely than either single mutant. Rhombomeres differ in how plastic they are. Transposition experiments showed hindbrain identity is partly committed early but can be re-specified by posterior environments. This supports a model of progressive determination rather than a fixed early prepattern.

**Evolutionary depth.** Lampreys show segmental Hox and Krox20 expression in the hindbrain, so the network predates jawed vertebrates.
levels.expert:
**Human disorders.** Hindbrain patterning defects present as congenital cranial dysinnervation disorders (CCDDs), brainstem hypoplasia and craniofacial anomalies:
- **HOXA1 biallelic loss**: Bosley-Salih-Alorainy syndrome and Athabascan brainstem dysgenesis syndrome. Features include horizontal gaze palsy, sensorineural deafness from inner ear malformation, internal carotid artery anomalies, and in some cases central hypoventilation and conotruncal heart defects.
- **HOXB1 recessive variants**: hereditary congenital facial paresis (HCFP3), a selective failure of facial motor nucleus development that mirrors the mouse r4 phenotype.
- **Möbius syndrome** (VI/VII palsy) is mostly nongenetic or vascular in origin. It overlaps phenotypically, and variants in PLXND1 and REV3L are reported. Genetic workup should distinguish Möbius from HOXB1 and HOXA1 disease.
- **EGR2 (KROX20)** variants mainly cause peripheral demyelinating neuropathy, reflecting its later Schwann cell role rather than its hindbrain role.

**Teratology.** Retinoid embryopathy shows clinically what happens when the RA–Hox axis is disrupted. Isotretinoin exposure produces microtia, cerebellar and brainstem hypoplasia, hydrocephalus and conotruncal defects. Animal models show anterior rhombomeres posteriorized (r2/r3 acquiring r4 character). This is why strict pregnancy-prevention programs such as iPLEDGE exist. RA deficiency (Raldh2 loss) conversely expands anterior identity.

**Neurosurgical relevance.** Rhombomeric origins explain nuclear topography seen on high-resolution brainstem MRI and diffusion tractography. These methods can identify absent or hypoplastic cranial nerves preoperatively in CCDD and in complex posterior fossa malformations. Pontine tegmental cap dysplasia and some forms of rhombencephalosynapsis likely reflect segmental or midline patterning failures. Their genetics remain largely unknown.

**Research frontiers.**
- Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics of human embryonic hindbrain are refining which human rhombomeric codes are conserved and which diverge from mouse.
- Brainstem organoids and assembloids derived from human stem cells use graded RA to generate Hox-patterned motor neuron subtypes. This is relevant to modeling CCDDs and amyotrophic lateral sclerosis bulbar vulnerability.
- Respiratory rhythm circuits (the preBötzinger complex, parafacial nucleus) derive from defined rhombomeres. This links patterning genes such as PHOX2B, mutated in congenital central hypoventilation syndrome, to postnatal breathing control.

**Pitfalls.** Single paralog variants often give mild or incompletely penetrant phenotypes because of redundancy. Imaging-negative findings do not exclude nuclear agenesis, so genetic testing and expert neuro-ophthalmologic examination remain complementary.

keyPoints: The embryonic hindbrain divides into about eight compartments called rhombomeres (r1–r8)
Hox genes encode homeodomain transcription factors that give each rhombomere its identity
Colinearity: gene order in a Hox cluster matches expression order along the body axis
A posterior-high retinoic acid gradient activates 3' Hox genes; Krox20 and MafB refine segments
Eph–ephrin repulsion keeps cells of neighbouring rhombomeres from mixing
HOXA1 and HOXB1 mutations cause human cranial nerve and brainstem disorders

test.q: What are rhombomeres?
choices: Swellings of the embryonic spinal cord
Layers of the developing cerebral cortex
Folds of the closing neural plate
Transient segments of the embryonic hindbrain
test.explain: Rhombomeres (r1–r8) are temporary, lineage-restricted compartments of the developing hindbrain.

test.q: What kind of proteins do Hox genes encode?
test.explain: Hox proteins carry a homeodomain that binds DNA and regulates target genes. Retinoic acid, not Hox proteins, is the secreted signal.

test.q: Spatial colinearity means that Hox genes at the 3' end of a cluster are expressed:
test.explain: 3' genes (paralog groups 1–4) are expressed in anterior regions such as the hindbrain; 5' genes are expressed further back.

test.q: Which signaling molecule forms a posterior-high gradient that activates hindbrain Hox genes?
test.explain: Retinoic acid made by Raldh2 in paraxial mesoderm and degraded anteriorly by Cyp26 forms the gradient that activates Hox genes through RAREs.

test.q: The transcription factor Krox20 (Egr2) is expressed in which rhombomeres?
test.explain: Krox20 marks r3 and r5 and is required for their formation. Hoxb1 marks r4.

test.q: Which molecules sharpen rhombomere boundaries by repulsion between alternating segments?
test.explain: EphA4 in r3/r5 and ephrinB ligands in even rhombomeres produce bidirectional repulsion that prevents cell mixing.

test.q: Facial nerve (VII) branchiomotor neurons are born mainly in:
test.explain: Facial motor neurons arise in r4, which depends on Hoxb1. The trigeminal comes from r2–r3.

test.q: In Hoxa2-null mice, the second pharyngeal arch skeleton:
test.explain: Loss of Hoxa2 causes a homeotic transformation: arch 2 elements become a duplicate of arch 1 structures.

test.q: Why can isotretinoin cause hindbrain and craniofacial birth defects?
choices: It prevents closure of the anterior neural tube
It blocks the folate pathway in neural cells
It inhibits Sonic hedgehog in the floor plate
It acts like retinoic acid and shifts Hox patterns
test.explain: Isotretinoin is a retinoid. Excess retinoid signaling posteriorizes anterior rhombomeres by altering Hox expression.

test.q: The rule that Hox gene order on the chromosome matches their order of expression along the body is called ___.
test.explain: Colinearity can be spatial, temporal, or based on sensitivity to retinoic acid.

test.q: How many Hox gene clusters do humans have?
test.explain: HOXA, HOXB, HOXC and HOXD contain 39 genes in total.

test.q: Retinoic acid is a molecule derived from vitamin ___.
test.explain: Retinoic acid is a vitamin A metabolite that acts through RAR/RXR nuclear receptors.

kidTest.q: What are rhombomeres?
choices: Tiny bones inside the inner ear
Little boxes in a baby's brain
kidTest.explain: Rhombomeres are a row of little segments in the baby's hindbrain.

kidTest.q: What do Hox genes act like?
choices: Labels that tell each box its job
kidTest.explain: Hox genes are like labels telling each segment what to become.

kidTest.q: About how many rhombomeres are there?
kidTest.explain: The hindbrain splits into about eight segments.

kidTest.q: What can happen if a label is missing?
choices: The brain turns a new color
The box builds the wrong thing
kidTest.explain: Without the right label, a segment can get mixed up.

kidTest.q: The back part of the brain is called the h _ _ _ _ _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: The hindbrain helps with things like breathing and chewing.

advancedTest.q: Hoxa1/Hoxb1 double mutants lose r4 identity more severely than either single mutant. This best illustrates:
choices: Spatial colinearity across the four clusters
advancedTest.explain: Paralogs partly compensate for each other, so phenotypes emerge clearly only when both are lost. This is also why single human variants can be mild.

advancedTest.q: Why is a graded retinoic acid signal alone insufficient to explain sharp rhombomere domains?
choices: Retinoic acid diffuses too poorly to reach neural cells
Retinoic acid is produced at the anterior end of the tube
Hox genes do not contain any retinoic acid response elements
Feedback loops convert the gradient into stable switches
advancedTest.explain: Networks such as Krox20 positive autoregulation and Hoxb1 auto-maintenance with Pbx/Meis turn a smooth gradient into sharp, bistable domains.

advancedTest.q: A child has bilateral horizontal gaze palsy, deafness with inner ear malformation and an internal carotid anomaly. The most fitting gene is:
advancedTest.explain: This triad matches HOXA1-related syndromes (Bosley-Salih-Alorainy and Athabascan). HOXB1 causes selective facial paresis; EGR2 mainly causes neuropathy.

advancedTest.q: Excess retinoid exposure would be predicted to make r2/r3 cells resemble:
choices: More anterior territory such as r1
More posterior rhombomeres such as r4
Floor plate cells of the spinal cord
advancedTest.explain: Retinoic acid activates more posterior Hox codes, so anterior rhombomeres are posteriorized. RA deficiency does the opposite.

lessons.title: Forebrain Signaling Centers: FGF8, Wnt and Retinoic Acid

levels.kid:
Imagine a big blank map of a new city. Some workers stand at special spots and shout directions: "This side is downtown!" "That side is the park!" Everyone nearby listens and builds the right thing.

The front of a baby's growing brain works the same way. Small groups of cells, called **signaling centers**, send out chemical messages. The messages spread out like the smell of cookies from a kitchen. Strong near the center, weaker far away.

Cells read how strong the message is. That tells them what to become: the front of the brain, the back of the brain, the eye area, or the part that thinks.

One messenger is called **FGF8**. Another is **Wnt**. A third is made from vitamin A. Together they help build the brain in the right shape.
levels.hs:
After the neural tube forms, its front end swells into the **forebrain**, which will become the cerebral cortex, the thalamus, the hypothalamus and the eyes. But how does each region know what to become? The answer is **signaling centers**: small clusters of cells that release proteins called **morphogens**.

A morphogen spreads out from its source and forms a **gradient**: high concentration nearby and low far away. Cells detect the local concentration and switch on different genes depending on how much signal they receive.

Three key signals pattern the forebrain:
- **FGF8** (fibroblast growth factor 8) comes from the very front of the forebrain, the **anterior neural ridge**, and later from a hub at the front of the cortex. It promotes front (anterior) identity, such as motor and frontal areas.
- **Wnt** proteins come from the dorsal midline, especially the **cortical hem**. They help build the **hippocampus** and must be kept low at the front. Wnt blockers made at the anterior end are needed for a head to form at all.
- **Retinoic acid**, made from vitamin A, helps set boundaries along the head-to-tail axis and shapes parts of the eye and forebrain.

A real example: in mice engineered to make extra FGF8 at the back of the cortex, a second, duplicated touch-sensing map of the whiskers forms. Changing the signal changes the map.
levels.college:
The forebrain (prosencephalon) is patterned by local **secondary organizers** that refine the broad identities set during neural induction. They act through **morphogen gradients**, controlling transcription factors that define areas.

**Anterior neural ridge (ANR) and FGF8.** The ANR, at the rostral edge of the neural plate, secretes FGF8. It induces telencephalic genes such as **Foxg1** (BF-1) and is required for the telencephalon to grow and survive. Later, the **commissural plate/rostral patterning center** keeps secreting FGF8 into the cortex.

**Anteroposterior repression of Wnt.** Posteriorizing Wnt signals must be blocked rostrally. The anterior visceral endoderm and prechordal tissues secrete Wnt antagonists (Dkk1, Sfrps), and the forebrain expresses **Six3**, which represses Wnt1. Without Six3 or Dkk1 the head is truncated. High Wnt instead specifies diencephalon and posterior identity.

**Zona limitans intrathalamica (ZLI).** This narrow boundary in the diencephalon secretes Sonic hedgehog and patterns the thalamus versus prethalamus.

**Cortical hem.** The dorsomedial telencephalon secretes Wnts (Wnt2b, 3a, 5a, 7b, 8b) and BMPs. These specify the hippocampus and choroid plexus. The antihem (pallial-subpallial boundary) releases antagonistic signals.

**Retinoic acid (RA).** Produced by Raldh enzymes (Aldh1a1-3) in the optic region, the head mesenchyme and the meninges. RA patterns the eye and ventral forebrain, while CYP26 enzymes degrade it rostrally to protect anterior identity.

**Cortical arealization.** FGF8 from the rostral pole sets opposing gradients of transcription factors:
- **Emx2** and **Nr2f1 (COUP-TFI)**: high caudal, promote visual and somatosensory fates.
- **Pax6** and **Sp8**: high rostral, promote motor and frontal fates.
FGF8 represses Emx2 and Nr2f1 rostrally, linking the secreted signal to the area map.
levels.phd:
Forebrain patterning combines early **anteroposterior (A-P) suppression of posteriorizing signals** with later secondary organizers.

**Head formation and Wnt antagonism.** In the classic two-signal model (Nieuwkoop's activation-transformation), neural tissue is anterior by default and is caudalized by Wnt, FGF and RA. Glinka and colleagues (1998) showed that **Dickkopf-1** induces heads in Xenopus. Mouse Dkk1 nulls lack anterior head structures. Six3 represses Wnt1 cell-autonomously (Lagutin et al., 2003), and in zebrafish **headless/tcf3** mutants (Kim et al., 2000) the forebrain is lost because Tcf3 repression fails. Wnt/β-catenin levels thus encode telencephalon versus diencephalon versus midbrain.

**FGF8 and the ANR.** Shimamura and Rubenstein (1997) showed that ANR explants induce Foxg1 in naive anterior neural plate and that FGF8-soaked beads mimic this. Hypomorphic Fgf8 alleles cause dose-dependent telencephalic loss. FGF signaling through Fgfr1-3 and ERK activates Sprouty and Spry/Dusp feedback, sharpening the domain.

**Arealization.** Fukuchi-Shimogori and Grove (2001) placed ectopic FGF8 posteriorly in the mouse cortex by in utero electroporation and generated a mirror-duplicated barrel field. Sequestering FGF8 with a soluble receptor shifted areas rostrally. This supports the **protomap** model (Rakic) over a purely thalamically driven **protocortex** model (O'Leary), though thalamic input later refines boundaries. Emx2 nulls expand rostral areas, and Nr2f1 cortical deletion (Armentano et al., 2007) produces a hugely enlarged motor area.

**Cortical hem.** Grove's group showed that Lef1 or Wnt3a loss abolishes the hippocampus. Lhx2 confines hem fate. In Lhx2 chimeras, ectopic hem induces extra hippocampal tissue, making the hem a true organizer.

**Retinoic acid.** RA binds RAR/RXR heterodimers on RAREs. The Raldh3-to-CYP26 balance creates localized RA sinks. RA from the meninges also drives cortical neurogenesis (Siegenthaler et al., 2009, in Foxc1 mutants), although whether the major effect is patterning or neurogenesis remains debated.
levels.expert:
Clinically, forebrain organizer biology shows up most clearly in the **holoprosencephaly (HPE) spectrum**, in **retinoid embryopathy**, and in **disordered arealization**.

**FGF8 and FGFR disorders.** Loss-of-function variants in FGF8 and FGFR1 cause Kallmann syndrome and normosmic hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. They also contribute to HPE and septo-optic dysplasia. These reflect the need for midline FGF signaling for olfactory bulb and GnRH neuron development and for ventral forebrain growth. Variable penetrance and oligogenic inheritance are the rule. A single heterozygous variant is often inherited from an unaffected parent, so counseling must avoid false determinism.

**Wnt-axis lesions.** SIX3 is a major HPE gene (with SHH, ZIC2 and TGIF1). Some variants act partly through failure to repress Wnt and partly via SHH regulation. Phenotypes range from alobar HPE to a solitary median maxillary central incisor within a single family. Gene panels and exome sequencing detect pathogenic variants in only a minority of non-chromosomal HPE, which suggests modifiers and environmental hits (the multiple-hit hypothesis, including maternal diabetes).

**Retinoic acid excess and deficiency.** Isotretinoin exposure in pregnancy causes **retinoid embryopathy**: microtia, conotruncal heart defects, thymic defects, and CNS malformations including hydrocephalus and cerebellar and posterior fossa anomalies, with later cognitive impairment. This is why strict pregnancy-prevention programs such as iPLEDGE exist. Biallelic loss of ALDH1A3 causes anophthalmia/microphthalmia. STRA6 (the retinol receptor) loss causes Matthew-Wood syndrome.

**Arealization and human disease.** NR2F1 variants cause **Bosch-Boonstra-Schaaf optic atrophy syndrome**, with intellectual disability, cortical visual impairment and sometimes polymicrogyria, linking the mouse area-map gene to human cortex. PAX6 haploinsufficiency (aniridia) can include absence of the anterior commissure and olfactory deficits.

**Open questions and tools.** Human cortical organoids rarely self-organize sharp areal maps. Engineered morphogen gradients from microfluidics or **organizer-like bead or cell implants** (e.g., SHH-producing "organizers" in organoids) are being used to recreate them. Whether human-specific expansion of the prefrontal cortex reflects altered FGF8/Sp8 gradient dynamics is unresolved. Single-cell spatial transcriptomics of fetal cortex now shows graded, not binary, areal identity before thalamic input arrives.

keyPoints: Signaling centers release morphogens that form concentration gradients
FGF8 from the anterior neural ridge induces Foxg1 and telencephalon
Wnt antagonists (Dkk1, Six3) are needed to keep anterior head identity
The cortical hem secretes Wnts and BMPs to make the hippocampus
FGF8 sets Emx2/Nr2f1 vs Pax6/Sp8 gradients that map cortical areas
Retinoic acid, controlled by Raldh and CYP26, patterns the eye and forebrain

test.q: What is a morphogen?
choices: A cell that migrates into the developing cortex
A signal whose concentration sets cell fate
A gene that repairs damaged DNA in neurons
A receptor found on the surface of mature neurons
test.explain: Morphogens form gradients, and cells adopt different fates depending on the local concentration.

test.q: Which structure at the rostral edge of the neural plate secretes FGF8?
test.explain: The anterior neural ridge secretes FGF8 and induces telencephalic genes such as Foxg1.

test.q: The cortical hem is especially important for forming the:
test.explain: Wnts and BMPs from the hem specify the hippocampus and choroid plexus. Loss of Wnt3a or Lef1 abolishes the hippocampus.

test.q: Why must Wnt signaling be suppressed at the front of the embryo?
choices: Wnt blocks the closure of the neural tube
test.explain: Wnt caudalizes neural tissue. Antagonists such as Dkk1 and Six3 protect anterior forebrain fate.

test.q: Mice lacking Dkk1 show which defect?
test.explain: Without the Wnt antagonist Dkk1, posteriorizing Wnt goes unchecked and the head is truncated.

test.q: Extra FGF8 placed at the back of the mouse cortex produced:
test.explain: Fukuchi-Shimogori and Grove showed that ectopic posterior FGF8 creates a mirror-duplicated somatosensory map.

test.q: Which transcription factor is high in caudal cortex and promotes visual fates?
test.explain: Emx2 (with Nr2f1) is graded high caudally. Pax6 and Sp8 are high rostrally.

test.q: Which enzymes degrade retinoic acid to protect anterior identity?
test.explain: CYP26 enzymes break down RA. Raldh enzymes synthesize it.

test.q: The zona limitans intrathalamica secretes which signal?
test.explain: The ZLI secretes Shh to pattern the thalamus versus the prethalamus.

test.q: Retinoic acid is made from which vitamin?
test.explain: RA is a metabolite of vitamin A (retinol).

test.q: FGF8 from the anterior neural ridge induces the telencephalic gene ___ (also called BF-1).
test.explain: Foxg1 marks and is required for the telencephalon.

test.q: A morphogen spreading from its source forms a concentration ___.
test.explain: High near the source and low far away, so cells read their position.

kidTest.q: What do signaling centers in the baby brain send out?
kidTest.explain: They release chemical messengers that spread out to nearby cells.

kidTest.q: Where is a message strongest?
kidTest.explain: Like a cookie smell, it is strongest near where it comes from.

kidTest.q: How do cells know what to become?
choices: They wait until the baby is born
They read how strong the message is
They copy the cell beside them
kidTest.explain: The strength of the message tells each cell its job.

kidTest.q: One messenger is made from which vitamin?
kidTest.explain: Retinoic acid is made from vitamin A.

kidTest.q: The messenger FGF8 helps build the front of the b _ _ _ _.
kidTest.explain: FGF8 helps shape the front part of the brain.

advancedTest.q: Ectopic posterior FGF8 duplicating the barrel field most directly supports which idea?
choices: Areas form through random cell sorting after birth
Retinoic acid is the main cortical area determinant
Thalamic axons alone assign cortical area identity
An intrinsic, signal-set protomap within the cortex
advancedTest.explain: Changing a cortical morphogen source reorganized the map, favoring the intrinsic protomap, though thalamic input later refines it.

advancedTest.q: A zebrafish mutant losing Tcf3 repressor activity lacks forebrain. The best explanation is:
choices: Derepressed Wnt targets posteriorize the anterior plate
Retinoic acid synthesis fails in the optic field
Sonic hedgehog from the ZLI is lost
Excess FGF8 overgrowth crowds out the forebrain
advancedTest.explain: Tcf3 represses Wnt targets anteriorly. Without it, Wnt-like posteriorization converts forebrain to more caudal fates.

advancedTest.q: Cortical Nr2f1 deletion would be predicted to:
choices: Shrink frontal areas and enlarge visual ones
Abolish the hippocampus by silencing the hem
Duplicate the thalamus through ZLI expansion
Enlarge motor areas at caudal areas' expense
advancedTest.explain: Nr2f1 normally promotes caudal fates. Its loss lets rostral motor identity expand, as Armentano and colleagues showed.

advancedTest.q: A heterozygous FGF8 variant is inherited from an unaffected parent by a child with HPE. Most consistent?
choices: Oligogenic or multi-hit causation with incomplete penetrance
Mitochondrial inheritance passed from the mother
The variant is benign and can be safely dismissed
Imprinting fully silences the maternal allele
advancedTest.explain: FGF8 and HPE genes show variable penetrance. Additional genetic or environmental hits explain unaffected carriers.
